newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds fall as dollar hits 4-year high on yen.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall as dollar hits 4-year high on yen.

text.p: Stocks tumbled Wednesday as market-leading technology shares sold off, while bonds fell sharply on worries about next week's Treasury debt auctions.
The dollar soared to a four-year high against the Japanese yen but fell against other major currencies.
The drop in the stock market came after Federal Reserve policy-makers decided to leave interest rates steady at the end of a two-day meeting.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 86.58 points, or 1.27 percent, at 6,746.90 after losing more than 120 points in a late sell-off.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,613 to 908 on heavy volume of 577 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index sank 25.31 points, or 1.84 percent, to 1,348.44.
Concerns that recent strength in the dollar could hurt corporate profits also came into play as investors rushed to take profits on their gains of the past month.

Analysts said the selling first emerged in technology shares and quickly spilled over into the broader market. Technology stocks were key drivers of Wall Street's January rally, which added almost 6 percent to the Dow.
"The momentum players that helped bring the market up are helping to bring it off," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Co.
Investors reacted to news that several brokerage houses had downgraded microprocessor heavyweight Intel Corp. and concern about slowing growth at computer networking giant Cisco Systems Inc.
"The market's run out of fuel here to push it higher," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage.
Prior to the sell-off, the blue-chip Dow was up more than 40 points as the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee, as expected, kept short-term interest rates unchanged.
Wall Street was also applauding President Clinton's pledge in his State of the Union address to seek a balanced budget.

But analysts said a larger immediate source of worry for the stock market could be the strength in the dollar, which could hurt future corporate revenues at multinational companies. A strong dollar lowers the value in dollar terms of U.S. companies' exports.
"If anything pushed people off the fence, it might be the strength in the dollar," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.

During the Asian session, the dollar vaulted above 123 yen and continued climbing in New York to 123.85 yen, its highest level since it hit 124.33 yen during the week of Feb. 14, 1993. In late New York trading, the dollar fetched 123.30 yen, up from 122.40 yen on Tuesday.
The dollar fell to 1.6430 German marks from 1.6457 marks.
Gold prices continued to slide to the lowest levels seen in more than three years before staging a modest late rally.
Prices dipped early, with a morning fix in London of $343.15, the lowest since September 1993.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange's Comex division, April gold closed unchanged at $346.40 an ounce, but not before posting a new contract low of $344.30.

Cocoa prices on New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange plunged for the second day in a row as speculators sold heavily amid plentiful nearby supplies. The key March contract ended off $22 a metric ton at $1,272.
March cocoa has tumbled $51 -- or nearly 4 percent -- in two days despite a pair of estimates projecting a global supply deficit in the 1996/97 season.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index rose 20.6 points to 4,281.5, a record close. The 225-share Nikkei average finished 128.36 points or 0.70 percent lower at 18,185.97.
